correctness.rationale: The forced switch has one-edge retention 1-2/n and creation 1/[n(n-1)]. Centering the sum gives the exact eigenmode 1-(2n-1)/[n(n-1)] of the full matching chain, without treating the count as Markov. Counting compatible ordered adjacency pairs gives E(S)_2=E(S)=2n/(2n-1), hence the claimed variance and all-lag covariance. The exact lag-one replay on 15, 105, and 945 matchings at n=3,4,5 gave 4/25, 20/49, and 44/81. Independently, disjoint k-tuples give the Poisson(1) initial law by factorial moments. For the path limit, the conditional expected birth and death counts are (2n-s)/[n(n-1)] and 2s/n. Stationarity bounds the probability of two deaths by E(S)_2/[n(n-1)] and reversibility gives the same bound for two births. A mixed event is bounded by four alternative reconnections per selected present short edge, so it is O(n^-2) in stationarity. Up to the time the count exceeds K, the next count can be maximally coupled to one grid step of the immigration–death chain: the conditional discrepancy is bounded by a constant times the conditional multiple-event probability plus O_K(n^-2) (the continuous-time chain has these single-jump probabilities to first order). Summing by stationarity for nT steps gives o(1) for fixed K; the expected initial count plus all births is O(1+T), so the probability of leaving the cutoff vanishes as K grows. The initial laws converge also in TV on the discrete state space. The limiting chain's finitely many jumps on a fixed horizon can be shifted to grid times in J1, since it has no fixed-time jumps. Thinning at survival probability exp(-2t) gives both limiting two-time formulas, including the void probability.
residual_risks: The bounded replay checks finite covariance inputs, not path convergence. The latter uses the uniform stationary initial law and is not asserted for arbitrary initial conditions.
